title: Northern Mariana Islands U.S. Workforce Act of 2018
official_summary:
Northern Mariana Islands U.S. Workforce Act of 2018

(Sec. 3) This bill extends by 10 years, through 2029, and revises the immigration transition program for the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI).

The Governor of the CNMI must submit to the Department of Labor, and Labor must approve, a plan for using fees collected for vocational education.

Labor must report on the number of asylum seekers it anticipates at the end of the transition program and its efforts to prepare for the asylum seekers.

The bill revises the Commonwealth Only Transitional Worker permit system, including to limit the validity of a permit to a one-year period, at most.

Employers petitioning for one or more such permits must pay a specified fraud prevention and detection fee.

Before an employer's petition for a permit may be approved by Labor, the employer must apply to Labor for a temporary labor certification that confirms (1) there are not sufficient U.S. workers in the CNMI who are able, willing, qualified, and available to perform the work involved in the petition; and (2) employment of the nonimmigrant worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed U.S. workers. Workers under permits must be paid the highest of CNMI minimum wage, federal minimum wage, or the prevailing wage for the occupation. The bill provides for renewal of permits and three-year permits for workers permitted since FY2015.

The bill caps the number of permits that may be issued each fiscal year. The cap is lowered each year.

summary.headline: Extends and revises the immigration transition program for the Northern Mariana Islands through 2029, with new rules for worker permits, wages, and labor checks.
summary.what_it_does: The law extends the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands immigration transition program by 10 years, through 2029. It limits Commonwealth Only Transitional Worker permits to one year at most, requires employers to pay a fraud prevention fee, and requires them to get a labor certification from the Department of Labor showing that enough qualified U.S. workers are not available and that wages and conditions for U.S. workers will not be harmed. It also sets a yearly cap on permits that gets lower each year, and requires workers under permits to be paid the highest of the CNMI minimum wage, federal minimum wage, or the prevailing wage for their job.

who_it_affects.group: Employers in the Northern Mariana Islands who want to hire transitional workers
who_it_affects.how: They must pay a fraud prevention fee, obtain a Department of Labor labor certification before a permit petition can be approved, and follow the wage rules.

who_it_affects.group: Transitional foreign workers holding Commonwealth Only Transitional Worker permits
who_it_affects.how: Their permits last one year at most, and they must be paid at least the highest of the CNMI minimum wage, federal minimum wage, or prevailing wage for their occupation.

who_it_affects.group: U.S. workers in the Northern Mariana Islands
who_it_affects.how: Employers must show there are not enough available qualified U.S. workers before hiring under these permits, and the Labor Department must confirm that wages and working conditions for similar U.S. workers will not be harmed.

who_it_affects.group: The Commonwealth government of the Northern Mariana Islands
who_it_affects.how: The Governor must submit a plan to the Labor Department for using fees collected for vocational education, and the Labor Department must approve it.

who_it_affects.group: Asylum seekers in the Northern Mariana Islands
who_it_affects.how: The Labor Department must report on the expected number of asylum seekers at the end of the transition program and on its preparations for them.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Enacted July 24, 2018; the program extension runs through 2029.
